analysis.one_liner: Loosens marine mammal protection rules to speed federal permits for offshore industry.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee approved the bill by voice vote in November 2018 and put it on the calendar of bills awaiting a floor vote, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies disturb whales, dolphins, and seals while drilling, surveying, or building at sea, they must get a federal permit and follow conditions designed to minimize the harm. This bill would relax those rules: it would let foreign companies apply, drop the limit on how many animals can be harmed, weaken monitoring and reporting requirements, and bar agencies from imposing any permit condition that changes a project's design, location, timing, or duration [S2]. It would also give the agency just 120 days to decide a permit — and if it misses the deadline, the permit is automatically approved on the applicant's own terms — and would exempt any harm covered by a permit from the Endangered Species Act [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that conduct offshore oil and gas exploration, seismic surveying, and marine construction. They would get faster permit decisions, weaker mitigation and monitoring requirements, automatic approval if the agency misses a deadline, and freedom from Endangered Species Act reviews of harm to marine mammals [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Offshore energy and marine construction firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets firm deadlines: the agency must accept or reject a permit application within roughly 45 to 75 days, and if it fails to make a decision within 120 days, the permit is deemed issued on the exact terms the applicant requested, with no conditions or further review [S3].

It removes the legal limits on incidental-harassment permits — the requirement that only a small number of marine mammals be affected and that the harm occur in a specific geographic region — and allows foreign companies to apply for the first time [S2].

It strips agencies of the power to require meaningful mitigation: any condition must cause no more than a minor change to the activity and cannot alter its basic design, location, scope, duration, or timing, and monitoring requirements must be 'efficient and practical' as the agency determines [S3].

It exempts any taking of a marine mammal that complies with a permit from the Endangered Species Act's prohibition on taking, and exempts federal agencies from consulting on impacts to endangered marine mammals and their critical habitat [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public, through weakened protections for whales, dolphins, and seals. Under current law, companies disturbing marine mammals must minimize and monitor the harm; this bill would remove the cap on how many animals can be affected, prevent agencies from requiring changes to projects that disturb them, strip endangered species protections for permitted harm, and let permits be approved automatically if the agency misses a deadline [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the 'small numbers' limit, so a single permit could authorize disturbing large numbers of whales, dolphins, or seals, and the statutory mitigation standard — requiring the least practicable impact on species and their habitat — would be deleted [S2][S3].

The automatic-approval clause works one way only: if the agency misses the 120-day deadline, the permit is granted on the applicant's own terms with no conditions, while applicants face no equivalent penalty [S3].

Exempting permitted harm from Endangered Species Act consultation would eliminate the separate review that currently checks impacts to endangered whales such as North Atlantic right whales and their critical habitat [S3].

The bill's stated purpose — cutting permitting delays that can slow legitimate coastal restoration and infrastructure work — is a real concern, but the bill addresses it by stripping protections rather than adding resources or staff to speed reviews [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Permitting delays for offshore work are a genuine problem, and deadlines can be a legitimate fix. But this bill goes far beyond deadlines: it removes the cap on how many marine mammals can be harmed, weakens monitoring and mitigation, strips Endangered Species Act review, and hands applicants automatic approval if the agency misses a deadline. The costs fall on wildlife and the public, while the benefits accrue to a narrow set of offshore industries.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee approved the bill by voice vote in November 2018 and placed it on the calendar of bills waiting for a floor vote, but the House never voted before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 29, 2017 by Rep. Mike Johnson of Louisiana and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1].

On January 10, 2018 the subcommittee was discharged and the full committee considered and marked up the bill, ordering it reported by voice vote; the committee formally reported it on November 16, 2018 and placed it on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 804), the list of bills awaiting a House floor vote [S5].
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Marine mammal protections stayed intact: the caps on how many animals can be harmed, the mitigation requirements, and the Endangered Species Act review all remain in force. Offshore energy and marine construction companies did not get the faster, weaker permitting regime they sought.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support; the committee approved it by voice vote, which leaves no record of how individual members lined up, and the House never voted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas exploration and seismic surveying
industries.note: Seismic airgun surveys and drilling activity harass whales and dolphins. The bill would remove the cap on how many animals can be disturbed, weaken mitigation and monitoring requirements, exempt permitted harm from the Endangered Species Act, and grant permits automatically if the agency misses a 120-day deadline [S2][S3].

Pile driving and other coastal construction projects must currently obtain harassment permits and accept mitigation conditions. The bill would guarantee faster decisions and bar agencies from imposing any condition that changes a project's design, location, scope, duration, or timing [S2][S3].
